paragraphs.heading: What they are
paragraphs.text: Sedimentary rocks form when sediments that gathered at Earth's surface are cemented together. Sediments are particles of minerals or of organic matter. Sedimentation is any process that makes these particles settle in place. It can also happen when dissolved minerals precipitate out of water.

paragraphs.heading: Where the sediment comes from
paragraphs.text: Mineral particles, called geological detritus, come from the weathering and erosion of existing rocks, or from blobs of molten lava erupted by volcanoes that then solidify. Water, wind, ice or mass movement carry this detritus to where it is deposited. Biological detritus is made of the bodies and parts, mainly shells, of dead aquatic organisms, together with their fecal mass. It hangs in the water and slowly piles up on the floor of water bodies.

paragraphs.heading: A thin but wide cover
paragraphs.text: Sedimentary rock covers 73% of Earth's current land surface. Yet by volume it is estimated at only 8% of the crust. It is a thin veneer over a crust made mainly of igneous and metamorphic rocks. Sedimentary rocks are laid down in layers called strata, a structure known as bedding, and often in large structures called sedimentary basins.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Studying sedimentary rocks and their strata tells us about the subsurface, which is useful in civil engineering, for example when building roads, houses, tunnels or canals. They are important sources of coal, fossil fuels, drinking water, ores and other natural resources. And the sequence of strata is the main source for understanding Earth's history, including the history of life.

paragraphs.heading: Four groups
paragraphs.text: Sedimentary rocks are sorted into four groups by the processes that formed them: clastic, biochemical, chemical, and a fourth group for others formed by impacts, volcanism and other minor processes. Clastic rocks are made of rock fragments, called clasts, cemented together. Clasts are commonly single grains of quartz, feldspar, clay minerals or mica, though they can also be fragments made of more than one mineral. Most types of limestone are built from the calcareous skeletons of organisms, corals, mollusks and foraminifera among them.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting by grain size
paragraphs.text: Clastic rocks are subdivided by their dominant particle size. Most geologists split loose sediment into three fractions: gravel (over 2 mm across), sand (0.06 to 2 mm) and mud. The rocks follow the same scheme: conglomerates and breccias are mostly gravel, sandstones mostly sand, and mudrocks mostly mud. A breccia is mainly angular gravel, while a conglomerate is mainly rounded gravel. Mudrocks, which are at least 50% silt- and clay-sized particles, divide into siltstones, mudstones and claystones.

paragraphs.heading: Clean and muddy sandstone
paragraphs.text: Once grains of sand size have been deposited, the gaps between them either stay open or fill with mud. A "clean" sandstone with open pore space is called an arenite. A muddy sandstone with abundant muddy matrix, over 10%, is called a wacke. A quartz arenite, for example, is mostly (over 90%) quartz grains with little or no clayey matrix between them.
